Caring for a cast iron pan

Seasoning

A cast iron pan lasts for generations when it is seasoned and kept dry. Seasoning is a thin layer of oil that has been heated past its smoke point until it bonds to the iron as a hard, dark, slightly glossy coat. Wipe a few drops of a neutral oil over every surface of the pan, inside and out, then rub almost all of it off again with a clean cloth. Put the pan upside down in a hot oven for an hour and let it cool in the oven. Repeat the whole cycle three or four times when the pan is new or has been stripped back to bare metal, and once in a while after that.

Cleaning

Clean the pan while it is still warm. Hot water and a stiff brush remove nearly everything; stubborn food comes off with a spoonful of coarse salt and a little oil. Soap is not the enemy that older advice makes it out to be, but soaking is, so never leave the pan in the sink. Dry it at once on a low burner until the last of the water has gone, then wipe a drop of oil around the cooking surface before it goes back on the shelf.

Rust

Rust is not fatal. Scrub it away with steel wool, wash and dry the pan, and season it again from the start. A pan that has been rescued this way cooks exactly as well as one that was never neglected, which is why these pans turn up in good condition at every flea market.
